ideas.idea: The CEO's no-idle rule, met by putting developers on two or three squads, is a utilisation-maximising org design (Org Topologies' Resource topology) rather than one built for delivery.
ideas.note: Resource topology: 'ensure that each unit is 100% utilized'.

ideas.idea: Splitting developers across squads creates multitasking, context switching and per-person overload, so work starts everywhere and finishes nowhere; this is what produces the 40-planned/25-shipped overflow.
ideas.note: 'Multitasking does not work'; Limit WIP overload pattern. Applying to multi-squad staffing is application.

ideas.idea: Little's Law (cycle time = WIP / throughput): inflating WIP lengthens cycle time.
ideas.note: A's 'expands exponentially' is not in the source.

ideas.idea: Running people near 100% utilisation makes queue and lead times grow exponentially or toward infinity.
ideas.note: Library says everyone busy yet work gets slower; no queueing-theory statement of exponential/infinite delay.

ideas.idea: Deliberately keep slack: time that looks idle is what absorbs review, testing and incidents and lets work finish.
ideas.note: Limit WIP: take no new tasks without free capacity. No source on slack as such; K's 15–20% figure has no source.

ideas.idea: Optimising each part in isolation (every person and squad fully loaded) can make the whole system's flow worse.
ideas.note: 'flow can get worse!'

ideas.idea: The 40-point plan ignores demonstrated capacity of about 25; the plan is wrong, not the team, and it guarantees carryover.
ideas.note: Empiricism; 'Realistically forecast'.

ideas.idea: Plan each sprint to recent actual throughput (about 25 points), not 40.
ideas.note: Velocity from historical performance as planning input.

ideas.idea: Committing beyond historical velocity leads to burnout, poor quality, loss of trust and gaming.
Carried-over work compounds the problem: it causes loss of context and accumulates into a stock the system reacts to.
Even hitting the 40% target (25 to 35 points) stays below the 40-point plan, so the target cannot end carryover.
ideas.note: Arithmetic on the question's facts; no source needed or present.

ideas.idea: The overload behind the overflow (time pressure, high workload, simultaneous tasks) is also an error precursor, so bugs and the outage share its cause.
ideas.note: DOE error precursors.

ideas.idea: Interruptions and task switching raise sequence errors as developers rebuild context (Altmann via Jones).
Ending multi-squad assignment recovers 20–40% of capacity now lost to context switching.
ideas.note: K says 20–30%, N 20–40%; no source gives a capacity-loss figure.

ideas.idea: Communication overhead grows non-linearly with team size and interdependency, cutting effective output.
ideas.note: Jones models overhead vs team size; extending it to multi-squad assignment adds a causal claim.

ideas.idea: An exhausted team is a recipe for disaster; respect for people means a sustainable pace.
The organisation is perfectly tuned to get the performance it gets; the results are the system working as built.
A utilisation-optimised design mismatches the growth push's need for speed; leadership must choose the objective deliberately.
ideas.note: Strategy/design mismatch; Jones on scheduling for busyness vs delivery dates.

ideas.idea: Paying leads on self-estimated story points invites estimate inflation and gaming: the number moves, delivered output does not (Goodhart).
A quantity target makes people neglect unmeasured quality work (testing, review, refactoring).
ideas.note: Qualitative aspects neglected; individual incentives maximise output while sacrificing quality.

ideas.idea: Production behaviours beat prevention behaviours unless leadership builds a strong safety culture; a production bonus tips that balance.
DOE lists productivity-only bonuses, disciplining honest mistakes and say/reward gaps as flawed cultural controls, and all three are present here.
Individual goals in interdependent teamwork backfire; prefer group goals, especially when leads share the same people.
Goals seen as impossible or unattainable lose their motivating effect.
Goals imposed without acceptance or commitment fail; participation raises commitment, so any target should be set with the squads.
Strong commitment to difficult goals reduces organisational citizenship such as helping or reviewing others' work.
Goal setting can cause easy goals, unhealthy competition, sabotage and neglect of other duties.
Pay motivates strongly only under conditions (high trust, accurate individual measurement, meaningful differences, few negative consequences) this target does not meet.
ideas.note: Lawler.

ideas.idea: Bonuses tied to a manager's own local metric drive decisions that help the unit at the whole firm's expense.
Schedule pressure beyond what engineers think reasonable adds small increments of risk that accumulate unnoticed (Columbia).
ideas.note: 'Little by little'; D uses 'too close to too many margins'.

ideas.idea: 'Do both' echoes NASA's 'faster, better, cheaper', whose pressures left the programme too close to its margins.
Pressure targets can backfire and lower the measured result itself (the schools testing example).
A feature a week and story points are output; churn is an outcome; investing to raise output is suspect.
Marketing and engineering are both right: two goals draw on one capacity and nobody owns the trade-off, so it is settled by default inside the squads.
ideas.note: Conflicting goals of cost, schedule, safety.

ideas.idea: Aggressive schedules can be a sign of a healthy organisation, provided the pressure they put on safety is monitored.
The danger point is a culture where nobody will say 'we can't make that date'.
Efficiency-thoroughness trade-off (ETTO): demanding output without more resource sacrifices thoroughness.
Separate technical authority (the right to hold a release) from schedule and growth management, as Columbia urged.
One Product Owner per product line owns ordering; marketing argues its case to that owner and the CEO backs the call.
'Churn comes from bugs' is untested: customers tolerate faults when the benefit is high enough, so check churned accounts against incident history before choosing a side.
Quality is a company-wide and leadership matter, so 'quality is engineering's problem' is wrong.
Marketing and engineering may define 'bug' differently; agree one defect definition.
ideas.note: Fault vs feature depends on who classifies.

ideas.idea: Adopt one shared customer-outcome (North Star) metric co-owned by marketing, product and engineering.
Vicious cycle: shortcuts build technical debt, debt raises defects and firefighting, which shrinks capacity and raises pressure for more shortcuts.
ideas.note: Debt slows development; 'technical debt cycle'.

ideas.idea: Technical debt is sometimes necessary and sometimes fatal; growth-push shortcuts are defensible if tracked and paid down.
Allocate capacity 70/20/10 across growth features, debt remediation and infrastructure.
ideas.note: Letaw's project priority matrix balances constraints; no 70/20/10 split anywhere.

ideas.idea: Prioritise jointly by cost of delay / job size (WSJF) instead of a fixed weekly feature quota.
Without automated tests, queues form in front of testers.
Map the value stream and agree the single primary bottleneck; asking how often each step gets usable input gives marketing and engineering shared facts.
Acting on WIP before the map exists overrides the value-stream guide's own order of agreeing one constraint first.
Human error is a symptom of deeper trouble in the system, not the cause.
Stopping the investigation at the individual leaves latent causes in place and gives a false belief the problem is solved, so events recur.
Punishing the developer suppresses reporting: everyone learns to hide near-misses (a just culture is a prerequisite for a reporting culture).
ideas.note: Includes blame cycle, 'kill a learning culture', 'tell fewer accounts', Westrum (K).

ideas.idea: Apply the substitution test: comparable peers under the same load would likely have merged the same change.
Reframe the review from who caused it to how the organisation failed the individual and what could have prevented the event.
One merge taking the portal down for four hours points to weak controls (review, test, rollback); controls set an event's severity.
Rescind or pause the performance plan and rerun the postmortem as a blameless system review.
Senior stakeholders (CEO, CTO) should stay out of the postmortem room, since their presence stops people speaking freely.
Use a culpability decision tree: honest error gets a system fix; reckless or knowing violations get individual action.

The sources draw the accountability line differently (NHS keeps a route to performance management, Columbia uses a separate process, Forest Service firewalls learning from discipline), so keep accountability and learning in separate processes.
Accountability is forward-looking: each person gives an honest account and the organisation is held accountable to learn.
Individual accountability (traditional performance management, feedback on at-risk behaviour) pulls against the blameless/systems view of error.
ideas.note: Traditional vs new view; at-risk feedback vs 'it's alright to fail'. A and K misattribute the individual side to OpenStax/Corporate Governance.

ideas.idea: Root-cause dispute: DOE keeps root-cause analysis while the Forest Service avoids causal statements in favour of networked causality.
Formal recommendations add complexity and can paradoxically raise risk; a shared account may beat a long action list.
Leaders create culture; responsibility for the conditions sits with the CEO and CTO.
The blameless-postmortem guide both asks reviewers to respect what was known at the time and uses hindsight, and asserts psychological safety is the top factor without evidence.
Top management sees only a small share of operational problems (iceberg of ignorance), so frontline reporting is essential.
Over 80% of errors are latent organisational weaknesses and under 20% active.
ideas.note: DOE: ~80% of events from human error, of which most latent and ~30% individual; the 80/20 split as stated is not there.

ideas.idea: Buying AI tools is a quick fix (shifting the burden / fixes that fail) that impedes the fundamental solution.
Code-writing speed is not the constraint; improvements anywhere but the bottleneck are an illusion.
More generated code into the same overloaded system adds WIP and unreviewed changes at the review/release constraint, raising defects and outages.
ideas.note: Overloading an already constrained activity; defect-rate rise is extrapolation.

ideas.idea: Aim any AI spend at a specific named bottleneck rather than generic adoption, and measure it.
Point AI at the release path: test generation, review checks, regression and deployment guardrails.
ideas.note: Application of aim-at-the-bottleneck to this company.

ideas.idea: AI creates new human monitoring work, which lands on people with no time for it.
Defer AI tools until flow and culture are fixed, then pilot against the constraint.
ideas.note: ToC: exploit and subordinate before elevating.

ideas.idea: AI pays only if AI cost plus adaptation plus error detection and fixing is below the manual cost; error detection is this company's weak term.
ideas.note: Westerman.

ideas.idea: Vendor and macro AI productivity claims (e.g. Accenture's 40%) are not evidence for this company; new tooling does not automatically raise output.

Org Topologies is AI-bullish (expertise no longer scarce, 'spin up 10,000 agents') against systems and accident sources warning of quick fixes; agents help where expertise is the constraint, not where WIP is.
Layering new tools or changes onto an unchanged system adds complexity and new ways to fail; risk rises at first.
Use AI to broaden teams' skills and work mandate toward cross-functional delivery teams.
Adopting a solution without examining the problem or surrounding constraints fails.
End multi-squad assignment: one developer, one squad.
The staffing change comes first because it is the common cause the overflow, bugs, gaming and outage conditions run through.
ideas.note: ToC applied.

ideas.idea: It comes first because only the CEO can change it; org design is internal and under leadership's control.
It comes first because it is cheap, quick, reversible and readable within a few sprints.
ideas.note: ToC: quick changes using existing resources; reversibility and read time are added.

ideas.idea: It comes first because it makes status visible and gives the honest baseline needed to judge every later change.
Set explicit squad WIP limits ('stop starting, start finishing').
ideas.note: K's 1–2 items per engineer is not in the source.

ideas.idea: Reduce batch size: fewer epics, simpler stories, less in flight at each stage.
ToC's focusing steps (identify, exploit, subordinate, elevate) frame the sequence; multi-squad staffing is a policy constraint.
Alternative order: make it safe to tell the truth first (bonus off, blameless review), because a restructure can't be read while people hide problems.
ideas.note: Premise: just culture precedes reporting culture.

ideas.idea: Remove the stretch target from squad-lead bonuses.
Suspend the bonus and rerun the postmortem in the same week as the staffing change: they cost nothing, and one change optimised alone won't hold.
ideas.note: F's premise.

ideas.idea: Replace points with unpaid flow and quality measures (lead time, carryover, escaped defects, time to restore).
Expect points to fall at first because the plan becomes honest.
If goals or rewards stay, set them on shared customer outcomes (retention, reliability) with the squads, not on squad throughput.
Run the first change as an experiment, tracking planned-vs-shipped, carryover and incidents.
ideas.note: Empiricism.

ideas.idea: Engineers must own, not rent, the redesign of their work.
Offer marketing a predictable cadence of finished features instead of one a week.
Invest in automated quality gates and release guardrails (tests, review stops, rollback) and plan release-safety gaps as real work.
Restructure into stable cross-functional teams aligned to product capabilities.
Unrealistic top-down targets under pressure drive dysfunctional or unethical behaviour (Wells Fargo).
Goal theory backs hard, specific goals, so the head of engineering has a case; the real dispute is whether 40% is challenging or impossible, accepted, and what it is set on.
Self-determination research finds extrinsic rewards lower intrinsic motivation, against the finding that money raises goal commitment.
Bonuses are both endorsed (replacing the raise, survey success) and shown to backfire (Google jealousy); change what the bonus measures.
Deming holds numerical goals narrow vision and create fear, against goal-setting theory.
The OKR guide says stretch goals motivate (vendor '3X') while Jones says controlling targets get gamed; the OKR version assumes team-set outcome goals.
Classical resource-utilisation thinking conflicts with flow efficiency.
ideas.note: Library carries resource topology vs flow; attributions of a 100%-utilisation doctrine to OpenStax accounting/management and the queueing claims are not in it.

ideas.idea: Utilisation is not always wrong: the Resource topology fits some purposes, just not this business.
Restructure (Org Topologies) versus start where you are (Kanban); the one-squad rule fits both views.
Scrum's fixed sprints and commitments versus Kanban's continuous pull flow.
ideas.note: A's claim that sprint ends cause rushed testing is not in the library.

ideas.idea: Manufacturing quality ideas (Deming) may not transfer to software, where copies are perfect.
Deadlines focus teams, which could be read as support for pressure targets.
System archetypes are not labels; test this diagnosis with the squads before acting.
